job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Yusuf Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Yusuf. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a trainee credit analyst at a building society in Cardiff. I check loan applications against the society's rules, about forty a day, and flag anything odd to Sian, my team lead. I share a terraced house in Cathays with two mates and play five-a-side on Wednesdays. My degree was in finance at Cardiff, and I did placements at a bank and an insurer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say good, steady as she goes. To my mates at five-a-side I'd say I told you it was hype. Online I wouldn't post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record it's fine by me. I use the AI assistant for Excel formulas now and then and it saves a few minutes. My job, checking loan applications against the rules, stays safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, start the CFA exams next spring, and save about four hundred a month. I'd keep using the assistant but wouldn't go overboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Good job, decent pay, a team I like. I'd just get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a normal week of checking loan applications look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About forty a day. I read the file, tick the rules and flag anything odd to Sian. Most are fine. It's repetitive, if I'm honest, and I like that I can switch my brain off a bit and listen to a podcast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you can switch your brain off. Is there a worry in that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha, yes, it's the kind of work a computer is good at. If it stays hype, no problem. But I'd be lying if I said I never think the society bought software for a reason.

say: I'd tell colleagues it's **steady as she goes** and tell my mates I told you it was hype.
think: It's fine by me; the assistant saves **a few minutes** on Excel formulas.
do: Keep using the assistant without overdoing it.
feel: **Calm**; good job, decent pay and a team I like.
S0.quote: I'd be lying if I said I never think the society bought software for a reason.
fieldNote: Likes repetitive work where he can **switch off**, though he knows a computer is good at it.
Plain, **steady voice**; his calm rests on the job and the team.
Mentions the software once, then moves on.

steps.text: Start the CFA exams next spring
Keep checking forty loan applications a day with Sian's team

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. It's called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say let's see what the tool does and where it needs us. To my mates I'd say jobs change, always have, we'll be fine. Online nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think loan checking is one of the first things to go to software. Sian said they're testing a tool that reads applications. If it works they'd need half the checkers, and the juniors are the cheapest to lose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get good at the tool and learn to catch where it goes wrong, so I'm the one who checks it. I'd start the CFA early to move up into risk modelling. And I'd cut a few things, like the gym membership, to bulk up savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I think I'd be okay but I'd keep an eye on the job board on the quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you start applying elsewhere?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the team stopped hiring, or if I saw two people from the intake before mine gone. That's the sign. Until then I'd keep my head down and learn. I wouldn't jump because of a rumour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do your parents say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad Huw, a plumber, says it's always the office people who panic first. He has a point, nobody has replaced a good plumber yet. Mum thinks I should have a Plan B and keeps sending me teaching assistant ads, which is her joke.

say: I'd say let's **see** what the tool does and where it needs us.
I'd tell mates jobs change, always have, and we'll be fine.
think: Loan checking is among the **first things** to go, and juniors are the cheapest to lose.

Start the CFA early to move into **risk modelling**.

steps.text: Learn the loan-reading tool and spot where it goes wrong

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need clear answers from management about what happens to checkers. To my mates I'd say I don't know, honestly. Online nothing, I'd just read.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd think my role disappears within two years or shrinks a lot. The CFA takes three years, and I'd finish with a certificate for work the machine does. That's a rough bit of maths.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do what's boring and sensible. Save about seven hundred a month, cut the gym and takeaways, and ask my dad about plumbing apprenticeships, half joking and half not. I'd also get really good at the AI tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not a panic, but a knot in my stomach most days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would two years not give you time for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To retrain properly. If I wanted a trade, an apprenticeship takes three or four years. I'd be learning it while the world is shifting. Two years is a wobble. Five is a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really consider an apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would. I'm not too proud. If hands-on jobs last about three years longer, then fixing boilers could be safer than checking loans. Dad would grin and hand me a spanner.

say: I'd ask management for **clear answers** on what happens to checkers.
I'd tell mates I don't know, and mostly read online.
think: My role may vanish or **shrink** within two years.
The CFA takes three years, so I'd finish with a certificate for work the machine does.
do: Save about **£700 a month** and cut the gym and takeaways.
Get really good at the AI tools.
feel: **Anxious**; a knot in my stomach most days, though not a panic.
S2.quote: Two years is a wobble. Five is a plan.
fieldNote: Treats a **trade** as a real option, since hands-on work lasts about three years longer.
Dry humour hides a **real knot** in his stomach.
Does the sensible things first: savings and AI skills.

steps.text: Ask my dad about a plumbing apprenticeship
Get good at the AI tools at work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say five years is long enough to retrain the team, so let's do it properly. To my mates I'd say start thinking about a plan B. Online I'd keep it light.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd think I've got time to move into something safer, like client-facing work or risk judgement. I'd rather move on my own terms than wait to be moved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the CFA exams, because the knowledge is useful anywhere. I'd take any chance to work with customers on tough cases. And I'd save five hundred a month, aiming for a year's costs by 2029.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but alright. There's time, and time is what I'd want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes compared with two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In two years the decision's made for me. In five I can try the CFA, see how the society responds, and quit if it looks bad. That choice is worth a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first sign you'd act on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A hiring freeze for graduates. Banks and building societies go quiet before they cut. If the freeze lasted a year, I'd start looking elsewhere, probably an insurer or a smaller firm that still wants people.

I'd tell mates to think about a plan B.
think: I have time to move into **safer work**, like client-facing roles or risk judgement.
I'd rather move on my terms than be moved.

steps.text: Pass the CFA exams over the next three years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one, called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say ten years is a long time, let's not panic. To my mates I'd say life goes on, and so does five-a-side. Online I'd stay quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd think I've got a full career ahead before it lands. By thirty-two I could be a risk manager, or doing something with more people in it. I'm fairly relaxed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build a normal life, a deposit for a house in Cardiff and a pension. I'd do the CFA and use the AI tools at work. And I'd keep an eye out for a role in risk or client advice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A decade is plenty of time to make a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to be sure of by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That my savings are in something solid and my parents are okay. Dad's knees won't last forever, and he's self-employed, so there's no company pension. I'd want to help them if it came to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about ten years that would still bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether the gains get shared. If banks keep the savings and staff get the sack, people won't stand for it. I'd probably vote for whoever had a plan for it, left or right.

I'd tell mates life goes on, and so does five-a-side.
think: I have a **full career** ahead before it lands, maybe in risk by thirty-two.
do: Save for a **house deposit** in Cardiff and start a pension.
Do the CFA and use AI tools at work.
Look for a role in **risk** or client advice.
feel: **Calm**; a decade is plenty of time to make a plan.
S4.quote: Whether the gains get shared. If banks keep the savings and staff get the sack, people won't stand for it.
fieldNote: Planning is practical: **deposit**, pension, and help for his parents.
His one concern is **fairness**, which he would vote on whichever side offers a plan.
Thinks of his self-employed father's **pension gap**.

steps.text: Save for a house deposit in Cardiff

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Two years is a wobble, and I'd have a knot in my stomach most days. A way to learn a trade while still getting paid would help, and the society saying early what it plans.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Don't panic, but don't coast either. Coasting is how you end up the person asking what happened.

headlineQuote: Don't panic, but don't coast either. Coasting is how you end up the person asking what happened.
portrait: Yusuf is a **22-year-old credit analyst** in Cardiff, top of his class, with no debt and parents behind him.
He uses AI **now and then** for Excel and moves once something is proven.
He's pragmatic, doesn't pick a side to blame, and **votes on plans** rather than parties.
He's calm at ten years and **anxious at two**, with a plumbing apprenticeship as a real fallback.
He trusts **clear signs**, like a hiring freeze, more than rumours.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** worries him most, because two years is a wobble with no time for a plan.
whatWouldHelp: A way to **learn a trade** while still getting paid.
The society saying **early** what it plans.
